label: lem:drift
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:drift}
	Almost surely $\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty$, while
	$\mathbb E\int_0^T|\alpha_s|^2\,ds=\infty$.
	More precisely, for every $t<T$,
	$\mathbb E|\alpha_t|=\sqrt{2/\pi}(T-t)^{-1/2}$ and
	$\mathbb E[\alpha_t^2]=(T-t)^{-1}$.
head: environment
name: Integrability of the information drift

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $B_T-B_t$ is centered Gaussian with variance
	$T-t$, we have $\alpha_t\overset{d}{=}N/\sqrt{T-t}$,
	where $N$ is a standard normal random variable.
	Using $\mathbb E|N|=\sqrt{2/\pi}$ and $\mathbb E[N^2]=1$, we obtain
	\[
	\mathbb E|\alpha_t|
	=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}(T-t)^{-1/2},
	\qquad
	\mathbb E[\alpha_t^2]=(T-t)^{-1}.
	\]
	Since the process $(|\alpha_t|)_{0 \leq t \leq T}$ is nonnegative, Tonelli's theorem
	yields
	\[
	\mathbb E\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds
	=\int_0^T\mathbb E|\alpha_s|\,ds
	=2\sqrt{\frac{2T}{\pi}}<\infty.
	\]
	As the random variable $\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds$
	is nonnegative and has finite expectation, it is
	finite almost surely.
	
	Similarly, applying Tonelli's theorem to the
	nonnegative process $(|\alpha_t|^2)_{0 \leq t \leq T}$, we obtain
	\[
	\mathbb E\int_0^T|\alpha_s|^2\,ds
	=\int_0^T\frac{1}{T-s}\,ds
	=\infty,
	\]
	which completes the proof.
head: environment

label: thm:PRP
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:PRP}
	The process $W$ in \eqref{eq:alpha} extends continuously
	to $T$ and is a $\mathbb G$-Brownian motion. It is independent
	of $B_T$, and
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:recovery}
		B_t=\frac{t}{T}B_T
		+(T-t)\int_0^t\frac{dW_s}{T-s},
		\quad 0\le t<T.
	\end{equation}
	Consequently,
	$\mathcal G_t=\sigma(B_T)\vee\mathcal F_t^W$
	up to completion for $t<T$, and also at $T$.
	Moreover, every $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal G_T)$ admits
	the unique representation
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:PRP}
		\xi=\mathbb E[\xi\mid B_T]+\int_0^T H_s\,dW_s,
		\qquad H\in\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G).
	\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Innovation and representation

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show that $W$ is a $\mathbb G$-Brownian motion.
	For $0\le s\le u<T$, the Gaussian regression
	formula, applied to the jointly Gaussian
	increments $B_T-B_u$ and $B_T-B_s$, gives
	\[
	\mathbb E[B_T-B_u\mid\mathcal G_s]
	=\frac{T-u}{T-s}(B_T-B_s).
	\]
	
	It follows that, for $s\le u<T$,
	$\mathbb E[\alpha_u\mid\mathcal G_s]
	=(B_T-B_s)/(T-s)$. Hence, by conditional
	Fubini's theorem, for $s<t<T$,
	\[
	\mathbb E\left[\int_s^t\alpha_u\,du
	\Bigm|\mathcal G_s\right]
	=\int_s^t\mathbb E[\alpha_u\mid\mathcal G_s]\,du
	=\frac{t-s}{T-s}(B_T-B_s).
	\]
	It follows that
	$\mathbb E[W_t-W_s\mid\mathcal G_s]=0$.
	Thus $W$ is a continuous $\mathbb G$-martingale on
	every compact subinterval of $[0,T)$.
	Since $\int_0^t\alpha_s\,ds$ is continuous and has finite
	variation (from Lemma \ref{lem:drift}) and $[B]_t=t$, we have $[W]_t=t$.
	By L\'evy's characterization, $W$ is a
	$\mathbb G$-Brownian motion on $[0,T)$ (see Theorem 39 in \cite[Ch II]{Protter2004}).
	
	By Lemma~\ref{lem:drift},
	$\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely.
	Therefore, the continuity of $B$ implies that
	$W_t$ converges almost surely as $t\uparrow T$ to
	$W_T=B_T-\int_0^T\alpha_s\,ds$. Moreover, for $s<t<T$, the increment $W_t-W_s$
is independent of $\mathcal G_s$ and has distribution
$\mathcal N(0,t-s)$. Since $W_t\to W_T$ almost surely
as $t\uparrow T$, the convergence of Gaussian laws
and the preservation of independence under almost
sure convergence imply that $W_T-W_s$ is independent
of $\mathcal G_s$ and has distribution
$\mathcal N(0,T-s)$. Hence, $W$ is a
$\mathbb G$-Brownian motion on $[0,T]$.
Since $B_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
the Brownian property also implies that
$W$ is independent of $B_T$.

	
	Next, setting $U_t=B_T-B_t$, we obtain
	$dU_t=-dW_t-U_t(T-t)^{-1}dt$.
	Applying the product rule to $U_t/(T-t)$
	gives
	$$
	d\big(\frac{U_t}{T-t}\big)
	=-\frac{dW_t}{T-t}.
	$$
	Since $U_0=B_T$, integration yields
	\eqref{eq:recovery}. As $W$ is constructed
	from $B$ and $B_T$, we have
	$\sigma(B_T)\vee\mathcal F_t^W
	\subseteq\mathcal G_t$.
	The reverse inclusion follows from
	\eqref{eq:recovery}. The identity at $T$
	follows by continuity and completion.
	
	
	It remains to establish the predictable
	representation property.\footnote{
		For related results on martingale representation
		under initial enlargement of filtrations,
		see \cite{Amendinger200}.
	} By the filtration identity,
	$\mathcal G_T=\sigma(B_T)\vee\mathcal F_T^W$.
	Since $W$ and $B_T$ are independent,
	finite linear combinations of random
	variables of the form
	$\xi=h(B_T)\eta$, with bounded measurable
	$h$ and $\eta\in L^2(\mathcal F_T^W)$,
	are dense in $L^2(\mathcal G_T)$.
	
	By the classical Brownian martingale
	representation theorem, we may write
	$\eta=\mathbb E[\eta]+\int_0^T H_s^\eta\,dW_s$,
	where $H^\eta$ is $\mathcal F^W$-predictable
	and square-integrable. Thus
	\[
	\xi=\mathbb E[\xi\mid B_T]
	+\int_0^T h(B_T)H_s^\eta\,dW_s.
	\]
	The integrand is $\mathbb G$-predictable and
	belongs to $\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$.
	
	For an arbitrary $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal G_T)$,
	choose a sequence of such finite linear
	combinations converging to $\xi$ in $L^2$.
	The conditional expectation is an
	orthogonal projection in $L^2$, and
	the It\^o isometry shows that the
	corresponding integrands form a Cauchy
	sequence in $\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$. Passing to the
	limit gives \eqref{eq:PRP}.
	
	Finally, if two integrands yield the
	same representation, the It\^o isometry
	implies that their difference vanishes
	in $\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$. This proves uniqueness.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Unlike the classical Brownian martingale representation,
	the initial term in \eqref{eq:PRP} need not be deterministic,
	since $\mathcal G_0=\sigma(B_T)$ up to completion.
	For instance, $\mathbb E[B_T\mid\mathcal G_t]=B_T$ for every
	$t\in[0,T]$, whereas
	$\mathbb E[B_T\mid\mathcal F_t]=B_t$.
	Thus, the same terminal random variable gives rise
	to different martingales in the two filtrations.
head: environment

label: prop:transfer
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Transfer identity

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:PRP}, we have
	$B_t=W_t+\int_0^t\alpha_s\,ds$ as
	$\mathbb G$-semimartingales. Since $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb G$,
	the process $Z^\mathbb F$ is also $\mathbb G$-predictable.
	Hence, by the decomposition of stochastic
	integrals with respect to semimartingales,
	for every $t<T$,
	$$
	\int_0^t Z_s^\mathbb F\,dB_s
	=\int_0^t Z_s^\mathbb F\,dW_s
	+\int_0^t Z_s^\mathbb F\alpha_s\,ds.
	$$
	Moreover, $Z^\mathbb F\in\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$, so the stochastic
	integral with respect to $W$ extends to $T$.
	The finite-variation integral also converges
	absolutely by \eqref{eq:transfercondition}.
	Passing to the limit as $t\uparrow T$ therefore
	gives the same identity at $T$.
	
	Substituting this decomposition into
	\eqref{eq:FBSDE} yields \eqref{eq:transferred}
	for all $t\in[0,T]$, up to indistinguishability.
	
	
	No uniqueness is asserted for \eqref{eq:transferred},
	since the transformed generator
	$\widetilde f(t,y,z)=f(t,y,z)-z\alpha_t$
	does not satisfy the standard uniform
	Lipschitz condition. In fact, uniqueness
	may fail even in
	$\mathcal S^2(\mathbb G)\times\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$,
	as shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:nonuniq}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
If $|Z_t^{\mathbb F}|\le C$ almost everywhere,
	then \eqref{eq:transfercondition} holds by
	Lemma~\ref{lem:drift}, since
	\[
	\int_0^T|Z_s^{\mathbb F}\alpha_s|\,ds
	\le C\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty
	\quad\text{almost surely}.
	\]
	The assumption $Z^{\mathbb F}\in\mathcal H^2(\mathbb F)$ alone
	does not ensure this integrability.
	Indeed, the usual Cauchy--Schwarz argument
	is insufficient, since
	$\mathbb E\int_0^T|\alpha_s|^2\,ds=\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:drift}.
head: environment
name: A useful sufficient condition

label: eq:GBSDE
title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal G_T)$ and let $g$ be
	$\mathbb G$-progressively measurable, uniformly Lipschitz
	in $(y,z)$, with
	$\mathbb E(\int_0^T|g(s,0,0)|\,ds)^2<\infty$.
	Then the BSDE
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:GBSDE}
		Y_t^{\mathbb G}=\xi+\int_t^Tg(s,Y_s^{\mathbb G},Z_s^{\mathbb G})\,ds
		-\int_t^TZ_s^{\mathbb G}\,dW_s
	\end{equation}
	admits a unique solution in
	$\mathcal S^2(\mathbb G)\times\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$.
head: environment
name: Well-posedness of a regular enlarged BSDE

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:PRP}, $W$ is a
	$\mathbb G$-Brownian motion with the predictable
	representation property. The classical
	existence and uniqueness argument for
	Lipschitz BSDEs, based on Picard iteration
	and a priori estimates (see
	Pardoux and Peng~\cite{PP},
	El Karoui et al.~\cite{ElKarouiPengQuenez1997},
	and Briand et al.~\cite{BriandEtAl2003}),
	therefore extends to the present filtration.
	Indeed, the martingale representation
	property and the usual stochastic integral
	estimates remain valid in $\mathbb G$.
	The possibly nontrivial initial sigma-field
	$\mathcal G_0$ does not affect the contraction
	argument, and uniqueness follows from
	the standard stability estimates.
head: environment

label: ex:linear
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:linear}
	Let $\xi=B_T$ and $f=g=0$. In the natural
	filtration $\mathbb F$, the unique solution is
	$(Y^{\mathbb F},Z^{\mathbb F})=(B,1)$, since
	$\mathbb E[B_T\mid\mathcal F_t]=B_t$.
	In contrast, as $B_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
	the unique $\mathbb G$-solution driven by $W$ is
	$(Y^{\mathbb G},Z^{\mathbb G})=(B_T,0)$.
	
	
	More generally, for any Borel function $h$
	such that $h(B_T)\in L^2$, the zero-driver
	solutions satisfy
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[h(B_T)\mid\mathcal F_t],
	\qquad
	Y_t^{\mathbb G}=h(B_T).
	\]
	If $h$ is bounded and measurable, then
	$Y_t^{\mathbb F}=P_{T-t}h(B_t)$, where
	$P_sh(x)=\mathbb E[h(x+B_s)]$ denotes the
	Brownian heat semigroup (see e.g. \cite{KaratzasShreve1991}).
head: environment
name: Different information, different solutions

label: thm:nonuniq
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nonuniq}
	For the terminal condition $\xi=B_T$, the BSDE
	in the enlarged filtration $\mathbb G$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:singular}
		Y_t^{\mathbb G}
		=B_T-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb G}\alpha_s\,ds
		-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb G}\,dW_s,
	\end{equation}
	admits at least two distinct solutions in
	$\mathcal S^2(\mathbb G)\times\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$, with absolutely
	integrable drift, namely
	\[
	(Y^{\mathbb G,1},Z^{\mathbb G,1})=(B,1),
	\qquad
	(Y^{\mathbb G,2},Z^{\mathbb G,2})=(B_T,0).
	\]
head: environment
name: Nonuniqueness for the transferred singular generator

title: Proof
body_md:
By the semimartingale decomposition established
	in Theorem~\ref{thm:PRP}, we have
	\[
	B_T-B_t=\int_t^T\alpha_s\,ds+W_T-W_t.
	\]
	Rearranging this identity shows that
	$(Y^{\mathbb G,1},Z^{\mathbb G,1})=(B,1)$ satisfies
	\eqref{eq:singular}. The second pair
	$(Y^{\mathbb G,2},Z^{\mathbb G,2})=(B_T,0)$ also satisfies
	the equation, since both integrals vanish
	and $B_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable.
	
	Both pairs belong to
	$\mathcal S^2(\mathbb G)\times\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$.
	Indeed, $B$ is continuous and $\mathbb G$-adapted,
	and Doob's maximal inequality, applied
	in the natural filtration $\mathbb F$, yields
	$\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|B_t|^2\le 4T$.
	Moreover,
	$\mathbb E|B_T|^2=T$ and
	$\mathbb E\int_0^T1^2\,ds=T$.	Moreover, the drift integrals are absolutely
	convergent, since
	$\int_0^T|\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty$ almost surely
	by Lemma~\ref{lem:drift} for the first solution,
	while the drift vanishes for the second.
	
	
	Finally, for every deterministic $t<T$,
	$B_T-B_t\sim\mathcal N(0,T-t)$, so
	$\mathbb P(B_T\ne B_t)=1$.
	Hence the two solutions are distinct,
	which proves nonuniqueness.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
This result does not contradict the classical
	uniqueness theorem for uniformly Lipschitz BSDEs.
	Indeed, the transformed generator
	$\widetilde f(t,y,z)=-z\alpha_t$
	has the random Lipschitz coefficient
	$|\alpha_t|$, which cannot be bounded by
	a deterministic constant uniformly in
	$t\in[0,T)$.
	Thus, the standard uniqueness theorem
	is not applicable. In particular,
	square integrability of $(Y^{\mathbb G},Z^{\mathbb G})$
	and absolute integrability of the drift
	do not suffice to ensure uniqueness
	for the transferred equation.
head: environment

label: prop:disintegrate
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:disintegrate}
	Suppose that the terminal condition and the
	generator admit jointly measurable representations
	$\xi=\xi^{B_T}(W)$ and
	$g(t,\omega,y,z)=g^{B_T}(t,W,y,z)$,
	where, for $\mu$-almost every $x$,
	$\xi^x$ is $\mathcal F_T^W$-measurable and
	$g^x$ is $\mathbb F^W$-progressively measurable.
	Assume that $g^x$ is uniformly Lipschitz
	in $(y,z)$, with a constant independent of $x$,
	and that
	\[
	\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbb E_W\Big[
	|\xi^x|^2+
	\Big(\int_0^T|g^x(s,0,0)|\,ds\Big)^2
	\Big]\,\mu(dx)<\infty.
	\]
	Then, for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the Brownian
	BSDE with data $(\xi^x,g^x)$ admits a unique
	solution $(Y^x,Z^x)$ in
	$\mathcal S^2(\mathbb F^W)\times\mathcal H^2(\mathbb F^W)$.
	The solutions can be chosen jointly measurable
	in the parameter and the Brownian variables,
	with $Z^x$ jointly predictable, and
	$$
	(Y^\mathbb G,Z^\mathbb G)=(Y^{B_T},Z^{B_T})
	$$
	is the unique solution of \eqref{eq:GBSDE}.
head: environment
name: Disintegration of regular BSDEs

title: Proof
body_md:
By the integrability assumption and Tonelli's
	theorem, the data $(\xi^x,g^x)$ satisfy the
	standard Lipschitz BSDE hypotheses for
	$\mu$-almost every $x$. Hence, the corresponding
	Brownian BSDE admits a unique solution
	$(Y^x,Z^x)$.
	

To construct a jointly measurable family, we use
Picard iteration on the product space introduced
above. Starting from
$(Y^{x,0},Z^{x,0})=(0,0)$, define, for $n\geq 0$,
\[
Y_t^{x,n+1}
=\xi^x+\int_t^T
g^x(s,Y_s^{x,n},Z_s^{x,n})\,ds
-\int_t^T Z_s^{x,n+1}\,dW_s.
\]
More precisely, setting
\[
\eta^{x,n}
=\xi^x+\int_0^T
g^x(s,Y_s^{x,n},Z_s^{x,n})\,ds,
\]
the Brownian martingale representation theorem
gives
$\mathbb E_W[\eta^{x,n}\mid\mathcal F_t^W]
=\mathbb E_W[\eta^{x,n}]
+\int_0^t Z_s^{x,n+1}\,dW_s$,
and $Y^{x,n+1}$ is then obtained from
\[
Y_t^{x,n+1}
=\mathbb E_W[\eta^{x,n}\mid\mathcal F_t^W]
-\int_0^t
g^x(s,Y_s^{x,n},Z_s^{x,n})\,ds.
\]

The joint measurability of the data ensures
that the conditional expectations can be chosen
jointly measurable in $(x,t,\omega_W)$.
The corresponding martingale integrands can
also be chosen jointly predictable by the
parametrized martingale representation
argument, using approximation by elementary
predictable processes and the It\^o isometry.

Since the Lipschitz constant is independent
of $x$, the standard BSDE estimates yield
convergence of the Picard iterates in the
integrated norm
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbb E_W\left[
\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Y_t^{x,n}-Y_t^x|^2
+\int_0^T|Z_s^{x,n}-Z_s^x|^2\,ds
\right]\mu(dx)\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Passing to suitable subsequences and
measurable versions yields a jointly
measurable family $(Y^x,Z^x)$, with
$Z^x$ jointly predictable.

	
	
	By the standard a priori estimates for Lipschitz
	BSDEs, there exists a constant $C>0$,
	independent of $x$, such that
	\[
	\mathbb E_W\left[\sup_{t\le T}|Y_t^x|^2
	+\int_0^T|Z_s^x|^2\,ds\right]
	\le C\mathbb E_W\left[|\xi^x|^2+
	\left(\int_0^T|g^x(s,0,0)|\,ds\right)^2\right].
	\]
	Integrating with respect to $\mu$ and using
	the integrability assumption, we obtain
	$$
	\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbb E_W\int_0^T
	|Z_s^x|^2\,ds\,\mu(dx)<\infty.
	$$
	
	Since $B_T$ and $W$ are independent, their joint
	law is $\mu\otimes\mathbb P_W$. Hence, by
	Tonelli's theorem,
	\[
	\mathbb E\int_0^T|Z_s^{B_T}|^2\,ds
	=
	\int_{\mathbb R}\mathbb E_W\int_0^T
	|Z_s^x|^2\,ds\,\mu(dx)<\infty,
	\]
	where the finiteness follows from the standard
	a priori estimates and the integrability
	assumption. Thus $Z^{B_T}\in\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$.
	
	It remains to verify that the parametrized
	solutions yield a solution in $\mathbb G$.
	For elementary jointly predictable integrands,
	evaluation at $x=B_T$ commutes with stochastic
	integration. By approximation in the integrated
	$\mathcal H^2$ norm and the It\^o isometry, this
	property extends to $Z^x$. Consequently,
	\[
	\left.\int_0^t Z_s^x\,dW_s\right|_{x=B_T}
	=
	\int_0^t Z_s^{B_T}\,dW_s,
	\qquad 0\le t\le T,
	\]
	up to indistinguishability.
	
	Evaluating the parametrized BSDE at $x=B_T$
	and using the representations of $\xi$ and $g$,
	we obtain
	\[
	Y_t^{B_T}
	=\xi+\int_t^T
	g(s,Y_s^{B_T},Z_s^{B_T})\,ds
	-\int_t^T Z_s^{B_T}\,dW_s.
	\]
	Therefore, $(Y^{B_T},Z^{B_T})$ solves
	\eqref{eq:GBSDE}. Uniqueness follows from
	the well-posedness result for regular BSDEs
	in $\mathbb G$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Conditionally on $B_T=x$, the original process
	$B$ has the law of a Brownian bridge from
	$0$ to $x$, with conditional mean
	$\mathbb E[B_t\mid B_T=x]=tx/T$ and covariance
	$\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t\mid B_T=x)
	=\min(s,t)-st/T$.
	In contrast, since $W$ is independent of
	$B_T$, its conditional law given $B_T=x$
	remains the Wiener measure $\mathbb P_W$
	for $\mu$-almost every $x$.
	Thus, the parametrization in
	Proposition~\ref{prop:disintegrate}
	is performed with respect to the innovation
	$W$, allowing the use of standard Brownian
	BSDE theory for each fixed parameter $x$.
head: environment

label: thm:reflecttransfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:reflecttransfer}
	Suppose that $(Y^{\mathbb F},Z^{\mathbb F},K^{\mathbb F})$
	solves \eqref{eq:FRBSDE} and satisfies
	$\int_0^T|Z_s^{\mathbb F}\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty$
	almost surely. Then the same triple,
	viewed in $\mathbb G$, satisfies the reflected
	BSDE driven by $W$, with terminal condition
	$\xi$, obstacle $L$, and generator
	$\widetilde f(t,y,z)=f(t,y,z)-z\alpha_t$.
	More precisely,
	\begin{align}
		Y_t^{\mathbb F}
		&=\xi+\int_t^T
		\widetilde f(s,Y_s^{\mathbb F},Z_s^{\mathbb F})\,ds
		+K_T^{\mathbb F}-K_t^{\mathbb F}
		-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dW_s,
		\label{eq:GRBSDE}\\
		Y_t^{\mathbb F}&\ge L_t,\qquad
		\int_0^T(Y_t^{\mathbb F}-L_t)\,dK_t^{\mathbb F}=0.
		\nonumber
	\end{align}
	The transformed drift integral is understood
	in the almost surely absolutely convergent
	sense.
head: environment
name: Transfer of reflection

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:PRP}, we have
	$B_t=W_t+\int_0^t\alpha_s\,ds$.
	Since $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb G$, the processes
	$Y^{\mathbb F}$ and $K^{\mathbb F}$ remain $\mathbb G$-adapted,
	while $Z^{\mathbb F}$ is $\mathbb G$-predictable and
	belongs to $\mathcal H^2(\mathbb G)$.
	
	As in Proposition~\ref{prop:transfer},
	the semimartingale decomposition gives
	\[
	\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dB_s
	=\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dW_s
	+\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\alpha_s\,ds.
	\]
	The stochastic integral with respect to
	$W$ is well defined, and the finite-variation
	integral converges absolutely by assumption.
	Substituting into \eqref{eq:FRBSDE} yields
	\eqref{eq:GRBSDE}.
	
	Moreover, the obstacle constraint
	$Y^{\mathbb F}\ge L$ is preserved since it holds
	pathwise. The process $K^{\mathbb F}$ remains
	continuous and nondecreasing, and the
	Skorokhod condition
	$\int_0^T(Y_t^{\mathbb F}-L_t)\,dK_t^{\mathbb F}=0$
	is a pathwise Stieltjes identity.
	Hence it is unchanged by the enlargement
	of filtration, completing the proof.
head: environment

label: ex:reflectednonuniq
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:reflectednonuniq}
	Let $\xi=B_T$, $f=0$, and consider the continuous
	$\mathbb F$-adapted obstacle $L_t=B_t$. The transferred
	reflected BSDE in $\mathbb G$ is
	\[
	Y_t=B_T-\int_t^T Z_s\alpha_s\,ds
	+K_T-K_t-\int_t^T Z_s\,dW_s,
	\]
	subject to $Y_t\ge B_t$ and
	$\int_0^T(Y_t-B_t)\,dK_t=0$.
	
	One solution is $(Y^1,Z^1,K^1)=(B,1,0)$.
	A second solution is given by
	\[
	Y_t^2=B_t+(B_t-B_T)^2+T-t,\qquad
	Z_t^2=1+2(B_t-B_T),\qquad K_t^2=0.
	\]
	Indeed, It\^o's formula yields
	$dY_t^2=Z_t^2\,dB_t
	=Z_t^2\,dW_t+Z_t^2\alpha_t\,dt$.
	Since $Y_T^2=B_T$, the second triple satisfies
	the transferred equation. Moreover,
	$Y_t^2-L_t=(B_t-B_T)^2+T-t\ge0$, and
	the Skorokhod condition holds since $K^2=0$.
	
	Both triples belong to the usual
	square-integrable solution spaces.
	The drift integrals are absolutely convergent
	by Lemma~\ref{lem:drift}, since both integrands
	$Z^1$ and $Z^2$ have bounded trajectories
	on $[0,T]$. Finally,
	$Y_t^2-Y_t^1=(B_t-B_T)^2+T-t>0$ for every
	$t<T$. Thus the transferred reflected BSDE
	admits at least two distinct solutions.
head: environment
name: Nonuniqueness of the transferred reflected BSDE

title: Example
body_md:
Let $T=1$, $\xi=B_1$, $f=0$, and consider
	the continuous $\mathbb F$-adapted obstacle
	$L_t=B_t+c(1-t)$, where $0<c<1$.
	The transferred reflected BSDE is
	\[
	Y_t=B_1-\int_t^1Z_s\alpha_s\,ds
	+K_1-K_t-\int_t^1Z_s\,dW_s.
	\]
	
	A first solution is
	\[
	Y_t^1=B_t+c(1-t),\qquad
	Z_t^1=1,\qquad K_t^1=ct.
	\]
	Indeed, $dY_t^1=dB_t-c\,dt
	=Z_t^1\,dB_t-dK_t^1$, and
	$Y^1=L$, so the Skorokhod minimality
	condition holds.
	
	A second solution is given by
	\[
	Y_t^2=B_t+(B_t-B_1)^2+1-t,\qquad
	Z_t^2=1+2(B_t-B_1),\qquad K_t^2=0.
	\]
	By It\^o's formula,
	$dY_t^2=Z_t^2\,dB_t$ and $Y_1^2=B_1$.
	Moreover,
	\[
	Y_t^2-L_t
	=(B_t-B_1)^2+(1-c)(1-t)\ge0.
	\]
	Thus the obstacle and minimality
	conditions are satisfied.
	
	Using $dB_t=dW_t+\alpha_t\,dt$,
	both triples satisfy the transferred
	reflected equation. They belong to the
	usual square-integrable solution spaces,
	and their drift integrals are absolutely
	convergent, since the corresponding
	integrands have bounded trajectories
	and $\int_0^1|\alpha_s|\,ds<\infty$
	almost surely.
	
	Since $K_t^1=ct$ whereas $K_t^2=0$,
	the two solutions are distinct.
	Hence nonuniqueness may occur even
	when the reflection mechanism is
	active for one of the solutions.
head: environment
name: Nonuniqueness with active reflection

title: Remark
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:reflecttransfer} establishes
	a transfer identity, not a general
	existence-and-uniqueness result for the
	transformed reflected BSDE.
	Indeed, the generator
	$\widetilde f(t,y,z)=f(t,y,z)-z\alpha_t$
	does not satisfy the standard uniform
	Lipschitz condition. Thus uniqueness
	cannot be inferred from the classical
	reflected BSDE theory.
head: environment

label: thm:value
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Conditional value of information

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\mathbb F\subseteq\mathbb G$, every $\mathbb F$-stopping
	time is also a $\mathbb G$-stopping time. Thus,
	for any $\tau\in\mathcal T_{t,T}^{\mathbb F}$,
	$$
	S_t^{\mathbb G}
	\ge\mathbb E[X_\tau\mid\mathcal G_t].
	$$
	Taking conditional expectations with respect
	to $\mathcal F_t$ and using the tower property,
	we obtain
	$\mathbb E[S_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	\ge\mathbb E[X_\tau\mid\mathcal F_t]$.
	Taking the essential supremum over
	$\tau\in\mathcal T_{t,T}^{\mathbb F}$ yields
	\eqref{eq:value}.
head: environment

label: prop:equality
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:equality}
	Fix a deterministic $t\in[0,T]$.
	Suppose that some
	$\tau_t^*\in\mathcal T_{t,T}^{\mathbb F}$
	is also optimal for the $\mathbb G$-problem,
	that is,
	$S_t^{\mathbb G}=\mathbb E[X_{\tau_t^*}\mid\mathcal G_t]$.
	Then equality holds in \eqref{eq:value}.
head: environment
name: Equality under a common optimal stopping time

title: Proof
body_md:
By the tower property,
	$$
	\mathbb E[S_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=\mathbb E[X_{\tau_t^*}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	\le S_t^{\mathbb F}.
	$$
	The reverse inequality follows from \eqref{eq:value} in 
	Theorem~\ref{thm:value}, proving equality.
head: environment

label: ex:strict
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:strict}
	Let $X_t=B_t$ on $[0,T]$.
	Since $B$ is an $\mathbb F$-martingale, the
	optional stopping theorem gives
	$S_0^{\mathbb F}=0$.
	
	In $\mathbb G$, consider the stopping time
	$\tau=T\mathbf 1_{\{B_T>0\}}$,
	which is admissible since
	$B_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable.
	The corresponding reward is $(B_T)^+$,
	so $S_0^{\mathbb G}\ge(B_T)^+$.
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb E [S_0^{\mathbb G}]
	\ge \mathbb E[(B_T)^+]
	=\sqrt{\frac{T}{2\pi}}
	>0=\mathbb E [S_0^{\mathbb F}].
	\]
	Thus the additional terminal information
	strictly increases the expected optimal
	stopping value.
head: environment
name: Strict value of terminal information

label: rem:pathwise
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:pathwise}
	The conditional comparison
	\eqref{eq:value} does not imply
	$S_t^{\mathbb G}\ge S_t^{\mathbb F}$ almost surely.
	
	To see this, let $T=1$ and $X_t=tB_t$.
	
	In $\mathbb F$, consider the stopping time
	$\tau=1/2$ on $\{B_{1/2}<0\}$ and
	$\tau=1$ otherwise. Since
	$\mathbb E[B_1\mid\mathcal F_{1/2}]=B_{1/2}$,
	the tower property gives
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\mathbb E[\tau B_\tau]
		=\frac12\mathbb E[B_{1/2}
		\mathbf1_{\{B_{1/2}<0\}}]
		+\mathbb E[B_1\mathbf1_{\{B_{1/2}\ge0\}}]
		&=\frac12\mathbb E[B_{1/2}
		\mathbf1_{\{B_{1/2}<0\}}]
		+\mathbb E[B_{1/2}
		\mathbf1_{\{B_{1/2}\ge0\}}]\\
		&=\frac12\mathbb E[B_{1/2}^+]
		=\frac{1}{4\sqrt{\pi}}>0.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Consequently,
	$S_0^{\mathbb F}\ge\mathbb E[\tau B_\tau]>0$.
	
	


Conditionally on $B_1=x$, we may write
$B_t=tx+\beta_t$, where
$\beta_t=B_t-tB_1$ is a centered Brownian
bridge independent of $B_1$.
The corresponding conditional optimal
stopping value is
$$
v(x)=
\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal T_{0,1}^{\beta}}
\mathbb E_\beta\left[\tau^2x+\tau\beta_\tau\right],
$$
where $\mathcal T_{0,1}^{\beta}$ denotes the
stopping times of the natural filtration
of $\beta$ taking values in $[0,1]$.
In particular, $S_0^{\mathbb G}=v(B_1)$
almost surely.

For $x<0$, we have
\[
0\le v(x)\le
\mathbb E_\beta\left[
\sup_{0\le t\le1}
(t^2x+t\beta_t)^+
\right],
\]
where $\mathbb E_\beta$ denotes expectation
with respect to the law of $\beta$.

To study the limit as $x\to-\infty$,
fix a continuous trajectory of $\beta$.
For every $\varepsilon>0$, continuity
at $0$ and $\beta_0=0$ yield
$\delta>0$ such that
$|\beta_t|<\varepsilon$ for $t\le\delta$.
Since $x<0$, we have
$(t^2x+t\beta_t)^+\le\varepsilon$
on $[0,\delta]$.
On $[\delta,1]$,
$$
t^2x+t\beta_t
\le\delta^2x+\sup_{0\le s\le1}|\beta_s|,
$$
which is negative for sufficiently
large $|x|$. Therefore,
$\sup_{0\le t\le1}(t^2x+t\beta_t)^+
\to0$ almost surely.

Moreover, for $x<0$, this supremum
is bounded by
$\sup_{0\le t\le1}|\beta_t|$,
which is integrable.
By dominated convergence,
$v(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$.

	
	Since $S_0^{\mathbb G}=v(B_1)$ almost surely,
	there exists $M>0$ such that
	$S_0^{\mathbb G}<S_0^{\mathbb F}$ on
	$\{B_1<-M\}$, an event of positive
	probability. Thus pathwise domination
	may fail, even though the conditional
	inequality \eqref{eq:value} always holds.
head: environment
name: Failure of pathwise domination

title: Remark
body_md:
Consider $T=1$ and the continuous,
	$\mathbb F$-adapted reward $X_t=(2t-1)B_t$.
	Suppose that stopping is restricted to
	the two dates $\{0,1\}$.
	
	In the filtration $\mathbb F$, since $X_0=0$
	and $\mathbb E[X_1]=\mathbb E[B_1]=0$, the optimal
	value at time zero is
	$$
	V_0^{\mathbb F}=\max\{0,\mathbb E[B_1]\}=0.
	$$
	In contrast, $B_1$ is already known at
	time zero in $\mathbb G$. The decision to stop
	at $1$ can therefore be made according
	to the sign of $B_1$, giving
	$$
	V_0^{\mathbb G}=\max\{0,B_1\}=(B_1)^+.
	$$
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb E [V_0^{\mathbb G}]
	=\mathbb E[(B_1)^+]
	=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
	>0=\mathbb E[ V_0^{\mathbb F}].
	\]
	This illustrates the strict advantage
	of terminal information when stopping
	is restricted to $\{0,1\}$. It does not,
	by itself, establish strict inequality
	for the unrestricted Snell envelopes.
head: environment
name: Value of information with restricted stopping times

label: prop:endpoint
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:endpoint}
	Let $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
	measurable with $h(B_T)\in L^2$.
	For the zero-driver BSDEs, the solutions
	in $\mathbb F$ and $\mathbb G$ satisfy
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[h(B_T)\mid\mathcal F_t],
	\qquad
	Y_t^{\mathbb G}=h(B_T),\qquad Z_t^{\mathbb G}=0.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb E[Y_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]=Y_t^{\mathbb F},
	\qquad 0\le t\le T.
	\]
	If $h\in C_b^1(\mathbb R)$,
	$h\in C_b^1(\mathbb R)$\footnote{
		$C_b^1(\mathbb R)$ denotes the space of
		continuously differentiable functions
		$h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ such that both
		$h$ and its derivative $h'$ are bounded.
	}
	 then
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}=P_{T-t}h(B_t),
	\qquad
	Z_t^{\mathbb F}=\partial_xP_{T-t}h(B_t),
	\]
	where $P_sh(x)=\mathbb E[h(x+\sqrt{s}N)]$
	is the heat semigroup, with
	$N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$.
head: environment
name: Endpoint payoffs

title: Proof
body_md:
We first consider the BSDE in the original
	filtration $\mathbb F$:
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}
	=h(B_T)-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dB_s.
	\]
	Since $h(B_T)\in L^2(\mathcal F_T)$,
	the process
	$M_t=\mathbb E[h(B_T)\mid\mathcal F_t]$
	is a square-integrable $\mathbb F$-martingale.
	By the martingale representation theorem
	for Brownian filtrations (see, e.g.,
	Karatzas and Shreve~\cite{KaratzasShreve1991}),
	there exists a unique
	$Z^{\mathbb F}\in\mathcal H^2(\mathbb F)$ such that
	$$
	M_t=\mathbb E[h(B_T)]
	+\int_0^t Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dB_s.
	$$
	Evaluating this identity at $T$ and
	subtracting the expression at time $t$
	gives
	$M_t=h(B_T)-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dB_s$.
	Thus $(M,Z^{\mathbb F})$ solves the zero-driver
	BSDE, and uniqueness yields
	$Y_t^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[h(B_T)\mid\mathcal F_t]$.
	
	We now consider the enlarged filtration
	$\mathbb G$. Since $B_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
	so is $h(B_T)$. Hence the constant process
	$Y_t^{\mathbb G}=h(B_T)$, together with
	$Z_t^{\mathbb G}=0$, satisfies
	$$
	Y_t^{\mathbb G}
	=h(B_T)-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb G}\,dW_s.
	$$
	This solution is square-integrable.
	Its uniqueness follows from the
	well-posedness of the zero-driver BSDE
	in $\mathbb G$, since $W$ is a $\mathbb G$-Brownian
	motion with the martingale representation
	property (Theorem \ref{thm:PRP}). Consequently, the tower property
	gives
	$\mathbb E[Y_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=\mathbb E[h(B_T)\mid\mathcal F_t]=Y_t^{\mathbb F}$.
	
	Finally, suppose that
	$h\in C_b^1(\mathbb R)$.
	Since $B_T=B_t+(B_T-B_t)$ and the
	increment $B_T-B_t$ is independent
	of $\mathcal F_t$ with distribution
	$\mathcal N(0,T-t)$, we obtain
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}
	=\mathbb E[h(B_t+\sqrt{T-t}\,N)\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=P_{T-t}h(B_t),
	\]
	where $N\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ is independent
	of $\mathcal F_t$ and
	$P_sh(x)=\mathbb E[h(x+\sqrt{s}\,N)]$.
	
	
	Set $u(t,x)=P_{T-t}h(x)$.
	By the classical heat-semigroup representation
	(see Karatzas and Shreve
	\cite[Sections 4.3 \& 5.7.B]{KaratzasShreve1991}),
	$u\in C^{1,2}([0,T)\times\mathbb R)$
	and satisfies
	\[
	\partial_tu(t,x)
	+\frac12\partial_{xx}u(t,x)=0,
	\qquad t<T,
	\]
	with terminal condition $u(T,x)=h(x)$.
	
	
	Applying It\^o's formula to $u(t,B_t)$,
	and using $d\langle B\rangle_t=dt$, we obtain
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		dY_t^{\mathbb F}
		=du(t,B_t)
		&=\left(\partial_tu(t,B_t)
		+\frac12\partial_{xx}u(t,B_t)\right)dt
		+\partial_xu(t,B_t)\,dB_t\\
		&=\partial_xu(t,B_t)\,dB_t,
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	where the last equality follows from
	the backward heat equation
	$\partial_tu+\frac12\partial_{xx}u=0$.
	
	Moreover, since $h'$ is bounded,
	differentiation under the expectation
	gives
	$\partial_xP_{T-t}h=P_{T-t}h'$.
	The resulting integrand is bounded
	and hence belongs to $\mathcal H^2(\mathbb F)$.
	By uniqueness of the Brownian martingale
	representation,
	$$
	Z_t^{\mathbb F}
	=\partial_xP_{T-t}h(B_t)
	=P_{T-t}h'(B_t),
	$$
	for $dt\otimes d\mathbb P$-almost every
	$(t,\omega)$, completing the proof.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The projection identity relies on the
	zero-driver structure and the fact that
	the terminal payoff is already known
	at time zero in $\mathbb G$.
	For nonlinear generators, conditional
	projection generally does not commute
	with the generator, so the projection
	of a $\mathbb G$-BSDE need not satisfy the
	corresponding $\mathbb F$-BSDE.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The preceding projection identity is specific
	to zero-driver endpoint payoffs. For more
	general BSDEs, projecting a solution from
	$\mathbb G$ onto $\mathbb F$ may modify both its drift
	and martingale components.
	
	Indeed, under suitable integrability
	conditions, the optional projection of
	$A_t=\int_0^t\vartheta_s\,ds$ satisfies
	\[
	\mathbb E[A_t\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=
	\int_0^t\mathbb E[\vartheta_s\mid\mathcal F_s]\,ds
	+M_t,
	\]
	where $M$ is an $\mathbb F$-martingale.
	Thus, even the projection of a
	finite-variation process may produce
	an additional martingale term.
	
	Related calculations and applications
	to BSDEs are discussed in an unpublished
	note by Jeanblanc~\cite{JeanblancPC}.
	For nonlinear generators, conditional
	projection generally does not commute
	with the generator, so the projected
	process need not satisfy the original
	BSDE in $\mathbb F$.
head: environment
name: Projection and filtration shrinkage

label: prop:financial_call
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:financial_call}
	
	Suppose that $0<K<S_0$. Then
	\[
	V_0^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[(S_T-K)^+],
	\]
	whereas
	\[
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]-V_0^{\mathbb F}
	\geq
	(S_0-K)\mathbb P(S_T\leq K)>0.
	\]
	In particular, terminal information
	strictly increases the expected
	optimal exercise value.
head: environment
name: Strict value of terminal information

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S$ is an $\mathbb F$-martingale
	and $x\mapsto(x-K)^+$ is convex,
	$X$ is an $\mathbb F$-submartingale.
	The optional sampling theorem
	therefore implies
	\[
	\mathbb E[X_\tau]\leq\mathbb E[X_T],
	\qquad
	\tau\in\mathcal T_{0,T}^{\mathbb F}.
	\]
	Since $\tau=T$ is admissible,
	\[
	V_0^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[(S_T-K)^+].
	\]
	
	
	In the enlarged filtration $\mathbb G$, the terminal
	asset price
	\[
	S_T=S_0\exp\left(
	\sigma B_T-\frac12\sigma^2T
	\right)
	\]
	is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable, since
	$\mathcal G_0=\sigma(B_T)$ up to completion.
	Consequently, the informed investor knows
	the terminal payoff $(S_T-K)^+$ at time zero.
	
	Let
	\[
	A=\{(S_T-K)^+<S_0-K\}.
	\]
	Since $S_T$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
	we have $A\in\mathcal G_0$. Define
	\[
	\tau^*
	=0\,\mathbf 1_A+T\,\mathbf 1_{A^c}.
	\]
	This random time is a $\mathbb G$-stopping time.
	Indeed, for every $0\leq t<T$,
	\[
	\{\tau^*\leq t\}=A\in\mathcal G_0
	\subseteq\mathcal G_t,
	\]
	while $\{\tau^*\leq T\}=\Omega$.
	Thus $\tau^*\in\mathcal T_{0,T}^{\mathbb G}$.
	
	By construction, the investor exercises
	immediately on $A$, when the immediate
	payoff exceeds the terminal payoff, and
	waits until maturity on $A^c$. Therefore,
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		X_{\tau^*}
		&=X_0\mathbf 1_A+X_T\mathbf 1_{A^c}\\
		&=(S_0-K)\mathbf 1_A
		+(S_T-K)^+\mathbf 1_{A^c}\\
		&=\max\{S_0-K,(S_T-K)^+\}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Since both $S_T$ and $\tau^*$ are
	$\mathcal G_0$-measurable, the payoff
	$X_{\tau^*}$ is also
	$\mathcal G_0$-measurable. Hence
	\[
	\mathbb E[X_{\tau^*}\mid\mathcal G_0]
	=X_{\tau^*}.
	\]
	By the definition of the Snell envelope,
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		V_0^{\mathbb G}
		&=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{
			\tau\in\mathcal T_{0,T}^{\mathbb G}}
		\mathbb E[X_\tau\mid\mathcal G_0]\\
		&\geq
		\mathbb E[X_{\tau^*}\mid\mathcal G_0]\\
		&=\max\{S_0-K,(S_T-K)^+\}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	
	Taking expectations on both sides yields
	\[
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]
	\geq
	\mathbb E\left[\max\{S_0-K,(S_T-K)^+\}\right].
	\]
	Using the elementary identity
	$
	\max\{a,b\}=b+(a-b)^+,
	$
	we obtain
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]
		&\geq \mathbb E[(S_T-K)^+]\\
		&\quad+
		\mathbb E\left[
		\big(S_0-K-(S_T-K)^+\big)^+
		\right].
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Since
	\[
	V_0^{\mathbb F}=\mathbb E[(S_T-K)^+],
	\]
	it follows that
	\[
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]-V_0^{\mathbb F}
	\geq
	\mathbb E\left[
	\big(S_0-K-(S_T-K)^+\big)^+
	\right].
	\]
	
	Now consider the event
	\[
	C=\{S_T\leq K\}.
	\]
	On $C$, we have $(S_T-K)^+=0$.
	Moreover, since $0<K<S_0$,
	\[
	\big(S_0-K-(S_T-K)^+\big)^+
	=S_0-K
	\qquad\text{on }C.
	\]
	As the integrand is nonnegative,
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		&\mathbb E\left[
		\big(S_0-K-(S_T-K)^+\big)^+
		\right]\\
		&\quad\geq
		\mathbb E\left[
		\big(S_0-K-(S_T-K)^+\big)^+
		\mathbf 1_C
		\right]\\
		&\quad=(S_0-K)\mathbb P(S_T\leq K).
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]-V_0^{\mathbb F}
	\geq
	(S_0-K)\mathbb P(S_T\leq K).
	\]
	
	Finally, since
	\[
	\log\left(\frac{S_T}{S_0}\right)
	=\sigma B_T-\frac12\sigma^2T
	\]
	and $B_T\sim\mathcal N(0,T)$,
	we obtain
	\[
	\mathbb P(S_T\leq K)
	=
	\Phi\left(
	\frac{\log(K/S_0)+\frac12\sigma^2T}
	{\sigma\sqrt T}
	\right)>0,
	\]
	where $\Phi$ denotes the standard normal
	distribution function.
	
	Since $S_0-K>0$, we conclude that
	$
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]>V_0^{\mathbb F}.
	$
	This completes the proof.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The processes $V^{\mathbb F}$ and $V^{\mathbb G}$
	are the Snell envelopes of the same
	reward under different filtrations.
	They therefore correspond to the
	first components of the respective
	regular zero-driver reflected BSDEs.
	
	The preceding comparison concerns
	optimal stopping under the fixed
	probability measure $\mathbb P$, rather
	than arbitrage-free prices in two
	financial markets. In particular,
	advance knowledge of $S_T$ may
	change the no-arbitrage properties
	of the underlying trading model.
head: environment

label: prop:financial_reflection
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:financial_reflection}
	
	The Snell envelope of $X$ in $\mathbb F$
	is given by
	\[
	V_t^{\mathbb F}=S_t+c(T-t).
	\]
	The corresponding zero-driver
	reflected BSDE has the unique solution
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		Y_t^{\mathbb F}&=S_t+c(T-t),\\
		Z_t^{\mathbb F}&=\sigma S_t,\\
		K_t^{\mathbb F}&=ct.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	
	Moreover, its transfer to $\mathbb G$
	satisfies the reflected equation
	with singular generator
	$-z\alpha_t$.
	
	By contrast, the regular
	zero-driver Snell envelope in $\mathbb G$
	satisfies
	\[
	\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]-V_0^{\mathbb F}
	\geq
	\mathbb E[(S_T-S_0-cT)^+]>0.
	\]
	In particular,
	\[
	\mathbb P(V_0^{\mathbb G}>Y_0^{\mathbb F})>0.
	\]
	Thus the transferred solution
	does not coincide with the regular
	optimal stopping value in $\mathbb G$.
head: environment
name: Active reflection and enlarged information

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $S$ is an $\mathbb F$-martingale,
	the process
	$X_t=S_t+c(T-t)$
	is an $\mathbb F$-supermartingale.
	Its Snell envelope therefore
	coincides with $X$.
	
	Furthermore,
	\[
	dY_t^{\mathbb F}
	=
	\sigma S_t\,dB_t-c\,dt
	=
	Z_t^{\mathbb F}\,dB_t-dK_t^{\mathbb F}.
	\]
	The terminal condition is
	$Y_T^{\mathbb F}=S_T$, and the obstacle
	condition is satisfied with equality:
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}=X_t.
	\]
	Hence
	\[
	\int_0^T(Y_t^{\mathbb F}-X_t)\,dK_t^{\mathbb F}=0.
	\]
	The uniqueness follows from the
	standard well-posedness theorem
	for reflected BSDEs in $\mathbb F$.
	
	Recall that
	\[
	dB_t=dW_t+\alpha_t\,dt,
	\qquad t<T.
	\]
	The process $Z^{\mathbb F}=\sigma S$
	has bounded continuous trajectories
	on $[0,T]$ almost surely, and
	\[
	\int_0^T|\alpha_t|\,dt<\infty
	\qquad\text{a.s.}
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\int_0^T|Z_t^{\mathbb F}\alpha_t|\,dt
	<\infty\qquad\text{a.s.}
	\]
	The transferred triple therefore
	satisfies
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		Y_t^{\mathbb F}
		={}&S_T
		-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\alpha_s\,ds\\
		&+K_T^{\mathbb F}-K_t^{\mathbb F}
		-\int_t^T Z_s^{\mathbb F}\,dW_s,
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	together with the same obstacle
	and Skorokhod conditions.
	
	
	On the other hand, since $S_T$ is
	$\mathcal G_0$-measurable, the informed
	investor knows the terminal payoff at
	time zero. Consider the random time
	\[
	\tau^*
	=
	\begin{cases}
		0, & S_T<S_0+cT,\\
		T, & S_T\geq S_0+cT.
	\end{cases}
	\]
	Since $\{S_T<S_0+cT\}\in\mathcal G_0$,
	it follows that $\tau^*$ is a
	$\mathbb G$-stopping time. Moreover,
	\[
	X_{\tau^*}
	=
	\max\{S_0+cT,S_T\}.
	\]
	As this payoff is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
	the definition of the Snell envelope yields
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		V_0^{\mathbb G}
		&\geq
		\mathbb E[X_{\tau^*}\mid\mathcal G_0]\\
		&=\max\{S_0+cT,S_T\}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Taking expectations and using
	$V_0^{\mathbb F}=S_0+cT$, we obtain
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\mathbb E[V_0^{\mathbb G}]-V_0^{\mathbb F}
		&\geq
		\mathbb E[\max\{S_0+cT,S_T\}]
		-(S_0+cT)\\
		&=\mathbb E[(S_T-S_0-cT)^+].
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Finally, since $S_T$ has a lognormal
	distribution with support $(0,\infty)$,
	\[
	\mathbb P(S_T>S_0+cT)>0.
	\]
	Therefore,
	\[
	\mathbb E[(S_T-S_0-cT)^+]>0,
	\]
	which establishes the strict inequality.
	
	
	Finally, on the event
	$A=\{S_T>S_0+cT\}$,
	which has positive probability,
	\[
	V_0^{\mathbb G}
	\geq S_T
	>S_0+cT
	=Y_0^{\mathbb F}.
	\]
	Thus the transferred first
	component cannot coincide
	with the regular Snell envelope
	in $\mathbb G$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
This example distinguishes two
	different operations. The first
	transfers an $\mathbb F$-reflected BSDE
	to the enlarged filtration by
	introducing the singular drift
	term $-z\alpha_t$. The second
	solves a regular zero-driver
	optimal stopping problem in $\mathbb G$.
	
	Although the transferred triple
	preserves the obstacle and
	Skorokhod conditions, it need
	not represent the Snell envelope
	under the enlarged information.
	The two equations have different
	generators, and their solutions
	need not coincide.
head: environment

label: prop:financial_european
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:financial_european}
	
	For the regular zero-driver BSDE
	in $\mathbb F$, the solution is
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}
	=
	S_t\Phi(d_1(t))-K\Phi(d_2(t)),
	\qquad t<T,
	\]
	where $\Phi$ is the standard
	normal distribution function,
	\[
	d_1(t)=
	\frac{\log(S_t/K)
		+\frac12\sigma^2(T-t)}
	{\sigma\sqrt{T-t}},
	\]
	and
	\[
	d_2(t)=d_1(t)-\sigma\sqrt{T-t}.
	\]
	The martingale integrand is
	\[
	Z_t^{\mathbb F}
	=\sigma S_t\Phi(d_1(t)).
	\]
	
	In the enlarged filtration $\mathbb G$,
	the regular zero-driver BSDE
	driven by $W$ has the solution
	\[
	Y_t^{\mathbb G}=\xi,\qquad Z_t^{\mathbb G}=0.
	\]
	Consequently,
	\[
	\mathbb E[Y_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=Y_t^{\mathbb F}.
	\]
head: environment
name: Conditional valuation of a European call

title: Proof
body_md:
The conditional distribution
	of $S_T$ given $\mathcal F_t$
	is lognormal. Standard Gaussian
	integration gives
	\[
	\mathbb E[(S_T-K)^+\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=
	S_t\Phi(d_1(t))-K\Phi(d_2(t)).
	\]
	Writing this expression as
	$u(t,S_t)$ and applying
	It\^o's formula yields
	\[
	dY_t^{\mathbb F}
	=
	\sigma S_t\partial_su(t,S_t)\,dB_t.
	\]
	Since
	\[
	\partial_su(t,S_t)=\Phi(d_1(t)),
	\]
	we obtain
	\[
	Z_t^{\mathbb F}
	=\sigma S_t\Phi(d_1(t)).
	\]
	
	In $\mathbb G$, the terminal payoff
	$\xi$ is $\mathcal G_0$-measurable,
	because it is a function of $B_T$.
	Therefore $(\xi,0)$ solves
	the regular zero-driver BSDE
	driven by $W$.
	
	Finally,
	\[
	\mathbb E[Y_t^{\mathbb G}\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=
	\mathbb E[\xi\mid\mathcal F_t]
	=
	Y_t^{\mathbb F}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The preceding identity is a
	concrete financial illustration
	of the conditional projection
	result for endpoint-dependent
	payoffs.
	
	In the natural filtration,
	the martingale integrand is
	generally nonzero, whereas
	the payoff is already known
	at time zero in the enlarged
	filtration and the regular
	zero-driver representation
	has a vanishing martingale
	integrand.
	
	These conditional expectations
	should not automatically be
	interpreted as arbitrage-free
	prices or replicating values
	in an insider trading market.

title: Research problem
body_md:
Establish a transfer theorem for reflected BSDEs
	with optional obstacles, incorporating both
	increasing processes $A$ and $C$ in the Mertens
	decomposition. Identify integrability conditions
	ensuring that the transformed equation is
	well defined and determine appropriate
	solution classes in which uniqueness may hold
	despite the singular information drift.
head: environment
name: Transfer of irregular reflected BSDEs

title: Research problem
body_md:
For an optional reward process $X$ and a
	Lipschitz generator $f$, investigate conditions
	under which the $\mathbb F$-optional projection
	of the $\mathbb G$-$f$-Snell envelope retains an
	$f$-supermartingale property. More generally,
	determine whether the projected process admits
	a reflected BSDE representation with an
	explicit correction term accounting for
	the additional terminal information.
head: environment
name: Projection and nonlinear Snell envelopes

title: Research problem
body_md:
Replace $B_T$ by a general random variable
	$L\in\mathcal F_T$. Under suitable density
	hypotheses, characterize the information
	drift and the associated innovation process.
	Determine conditions under which the
	innovation retains the predictable
	representation property, and investigate
	existence and uniqueness for the corresponding
	reflected BSDEs, including those with
	irregular obstacles.
